headline: Fujitsu has a diamond-spin quantum computer working — and has not said how big it is
dek: Tin-vacancy centres built into photonic integrated circuits, running at −271.6 °C. The temperature is the interesting number. The missing qubit count is the interesting silence.

source.name: The Quantum Insider
source.title: Fujitsu develops diamond-spin quantum computer prototype, 8 September 2026 (reporting Fujitsu's own announcement)

body_html:
Fujitsu announced what it describes as the first working prototype of a diamond-spin quantum computer built by putting tin-vacancy (SnV) centres into photonic integrated circuits — the product of a collaboration with Delft University of Technology and QuTech running since 2020. It is reachable through Fujitsu's Hybrid Quantum Computing Platform.

The number that carries real information is the operating temperature: −271.6 °C, about 1.6 kelvin, against roughly −273.13 °C (about 0.02 K) for superconducting machines. Nearly two orders of magnitude in absolute temperature is not cosmetic: cooling power gets dramatically cheaper as you climb away from millikelvin, and cooling budget is one of the quiet constraints on how large any of these systems can grow.

Fujitsu's stated path from here is a multi-module prototype in 2027, 250 logical qubits by fiscal 2030 and 1,000 by fiscal 2035, eventually integrated with its superconducting machines. QuTech's Dr Kees Eijkel, quoted in the coverage, described demonstrating the scalability this approach needs as "a long and challenging journey" — which is the correct framing and worth more than the headline.

What this does NOT mean

  • It is not room temperature. 1.6 K is still deep cryogenics. It is meaningfully easier to reach than 20 millikelvin, and it is nowhere near a machine you plug into a wall.
  • No qubit count was published, so this prototype cannot be compared with any other machine on size. When a hardware announcement omits the count, the count is not the story the announcer wants told.
  • The 2030 and 2035 figures are a roadmap, not a result. They are dated, public and falsifiable, which makes them exactly the kind of statement the Ledger exists to track — and it is worth noticing they sit five and ten years out.
  • A new modality is not automatically a better one. Every platform trades something: this one is fighting the same photon-loss problem every photonic architecture fights.
concept_card_html:
Concepts in this story

Each of these is already explained on SymbiQ. Depth chips say how deep the explanation goes.

  • photonic qubitsworkingRoom temperature and natural networking, fighting loss as the central enemy.
  • logical qubitplainOne reliable qubit built out of many unreliable ones. The only qubit count that means anything.
  • gate fidelityformalThe metric that actually beats qubit count when you are reading a hardware announcement.
  • fault toleranceformalComputing reliably out of unreliable parts -- the regime the whole roadmap is aimed at.
